slides.heading: Oral Lesson
bullets: In the sentence “Fishes swim,” the subject is “Fishes” and the predicate is “swim.”
Is there any copula expressed?  There is not.
The predicate, then, can be affirmed of the subject directly — one word expressing both the copula and the predicate.
A word which can be used to affirm something of a subject is called a Verb.
It usually expresses action, being, or state:  I run (action);  I am (being);  I sleep (state).

rows.label: Action
rows.text: The subject does something — a deed or a motion.

rows.label: Being
rows.text: The verb be — asserts that the subject exists, or links it to what it is.

rows.label: State
rows.text: The subject is in a condition — neither acting nor merely existing.

slides.text: A Verb is a word which expresses action, being, or state.

slides.heading: How to Know a Verb
bullets: Ask:  does the word affirm something of the subject?  If so, it is a verb.
“Horses trot.”  — “trot” is a verb; it affirms action of the subject “horses.”
“Houses stand.”  — “stand” is a verb; it affirms state of the subject “houses.”
Cross out the verb and the sentence falls apart:  “The dog ___ the ball.”
Every complete sentence must contain a verb — the word that tells what the subject does or is.

slides.heading: Practice — Find the Verb
slides.instruction: Name the verb in each sentence.  (Just find it — don't worry about its class yet.)

slides.heading: The Object
bullets: In “Boys study grammar,” the word “grammar” is required to complete the meaning of the predicate “study.”
It tells what the boys study, and so completes the verb's meaning.
Such a completing word is called the Objective Element, or Object.
Ex. — Fire burns wood.   (burns what? — wood, the object)

slides.text: An Objective Element is a word or a group of words which completes the meaning of a verb.
examples: The dog buried a bone.  (object — a bone)

slides.text: A Transitive Verb requires the addition of an object to complete its meaning.
examples: Maria painted the fence.  (painted what? — the fence)
The dog buried a bone.  (buried what? — a bone)

slides.heading: More on Transitive Verbs
bullets: The object receives the action of the verb.
Test — ask “verb + what?” or “verb + whom?”  If there is an answer, the verb is transitive:  “discovered what? America.”
Rem. — The object is not always expressed:  “The child reads.”  (reads what? — the object is understood.)
Even then, an object can always be supplied — some word other than the subject:  “The child reads [books].”
Caution — a describing word after a copulative verb answers “what?” too (“remains what? — open”), yet it is a predicate, not an object.

slides.text: An Intransitive Verb does not require the addition of an object to complete its meaning.
examples: The children ran home.  (ran what? — nothing; “home” only tells where)

slides.heading: More on Intransitive Verbs
bullets: The action stops with the subject; nothing receives it.
Test — ask “verb + what?”  If there is no answer, the verb is intransitive:  “run what? — nothing.”
Rem. — Some verbs are transitive in one sense and intransitive in another.
Ex. — “She reads books” (transitive) but “She reads well” (intransitive).
To be sure whether a verb may be used both ways, consult a dictionary.
Ex. — Houses stand.   Boys swim.   (nothing is acted upon)

slides.text: A Copulative Verb is used to join a predicate to a subject, and to make an assertion.

slides.heading: The Copula Is Always a Verb
bullets: A copulative verb links the subject to a word that describes or renames it, and asserts it.
That word is the predicate, not an object — “The gate remains open”:  “open” describes the gate, so it is a predicate.
Recall Lesson 1:  the copula is the asserting word — “Iron | is : heavy.”
The copula is always a verb.
Common copulative verbs — am, is, are, was, were, be, become, seem, appear; and feel, taste, look, smell, sound when they link.

slides.heading: The Three Classes at a Glance
bullets: Transitive — passes the action to an object:   Dogs chase cats.
Intransitive — the action has no object:   Dogs bark.
Copulative — links the subject to a describing word and asserts it:   Dogs are loyal.
Notice: the same subject can take all three — it all depends on the verb.

slides.heading: Practice — Point Out the Verbs (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Point out the verb and tell whether it is transitive, intransitive, or copulative.  (Look hard — some verbs change class, and length is no clue.)

slides.heading: Practice — Point Out the Verbs (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Point out the verb and tell whether it is transitive, intransitive, or copulative.  (The same verb can belong to different classes — decide from the work it does here.)

slides.heading: Analyze — Copular Sentences {s,c,p}
slides.instruction: Model — “Iron | is : heavy.”  Split into subject | copula : predicate.  (Even tastes, became, and looks serve as copulas — the copula asserts, but is not itself the predicate.)

slides.heading: Analyze — Diagram the Sentence (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Model — “Scholars | learn | lessons.”  Split it into subject | predicate | object.  The line between subject and predicate reaches below the baseline.

slides.heading: Analyze — Diagram the Sentence (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Split each sentence into subject | predicate | object.  Remember: the divider after the subject reaches below the baseline.

slides.heading: Incorrect Language — Cautions
bullets: I. — After has, have, or had, use seen and gone — never saw or went:  “I have seen it.”
II. — For simple past time, use saw — never see or seen:  “I saw a dog.”
III. — For simple past time, use did and came — never done or come:  “He did his work.”  “Father came home.”
IV. — When the subject names more than one, use are or were — never is, was, or has been:  “The horse and the cow are in the stable.”
V. — When the subject is you, use were — never was:  “You were there.”

slides.heading: Practice — Fix the Verb (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Each sentence has a verb mistake. Give the correct word.
items: I have saw a fine horse today.
He done his work well yesterday.
The horse and the cow is in the stable.
My father come home last week.
I seen John at the fair.
George has went there several times.

slides.heading: Practice — Fix the Verb (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Each sentence has a verb mistake — one has two. Give the correct word(s).
items: Have you saw Mr. Olds today?
It is the largest peach I ever see.
I done my task before Eli come.
Eliza and Sarah has been here.
Perhaps you was trying to hide.
The little boy has went into the woods.
Hiram see a flock of wild turkeys yesterday.
Is a transitive verb's object always expressed?
answers: A word that expresses action, being, or state.
A word or group of words which completes the meaning of a verb.
One that requires an object to complete its meaning.
One that does not require an object to complete its meaning.
One that joins a predicate to a subject and makes an assertion.
No — “The child reads.”  (the object is understood.)
Only with a helping verb — has, have, or had.
